Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Kwame Osei is a sixty-five-year-old retail worker who has spent the last four decades stocking shelves and assisting customers at a discount department store in a midsized Midwestern town. Married for thirty-eight years, he lives with his wife in a quiet neighborhood that once felt safe. That changed on a humid June afternoon three years ago, when an EF‑3 tornado tore through the strip mall where he worked. The storm hit without warning. He was in the back room when the sirens blared; he ran toward the front, but the glass doors exploded inward and the ceiling began to peel away. He pressed himself flat behind an overturned display rack, debris hammering the metal, and for what felt like minutes he was certain the building would collapse on him. He remembers the roar and the pressure in his ears, the way the air turned black with dust. When it was over, he crawled out through a gap in the wall, unharmed but shaking. He has not felt safe since.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that afternoon refused to settle. It returned not as a recollection but as a full sensory re-experience: he would be folding shirts and suddenly he could hear the wind, smell the wet plaster, feel the weight of the rack against his spine. The memory played like a film he could not stop, always the same sequence of shattering glass and buckling ceiling, and each time it felt as if the tornado was happening right then, in the present, not something that had finished. He began to avoid the back of the store, and he stopped walking past the front doors during his break. More than that, he started to scan every room he entered for an exit: the break room, the restroom, even his own living room. As soon as he crossed a threshold, his eyes found the door and he calculated the shortest path to it. He had to know he could get out.

Kwame came to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that a catastrophe could arrive without warning at any moment. He told himself that he had to be on guard all the time, that if he relaxed even for a second the next disaster would catch him. He began to see danger in ordinary sights: a dark cloud on the horizon, a sudden gust of wind, the hum of an air conditioner that sounded like the storm’s approach. At work, he positioned himself near the emergency exit at the back of the sales floor so that he could slip out quickly. When customers asked for help in the front aisles, he felt a tightness in his chest and often sent them toward a younger colleague. He started carrying a small radio to check the weather, and he would turn it on whenever he felt the air pressure shift, distracting himself with the forecast instead of the panic rising in his throat.

At night, sleep became a battle. He lay awake, listening, alert for the first hint of wind or a distant rumble. His wife would find him sitting up at three in the morning, staring at the window. He told her he needed to stay watchful, that something could happen any minute. She grew frustrated and worried; their evenings turned silent. He felt he had changed permanently for the worse, that the man who used to joke with customers and sleep through thunderstorms was gone, and he could not find a way back. His hypervigilance exhausted him, but when he tried to stop checking his surroundings, the anxiety spiked so sharply that he could not think.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment in the break room six weeks ago. A coworker slammed a metal cabinet door, and Kwame dropped to the floor, heart hammering, certain that the roof was coming down. The coworker helped him up, but the shame was crushing. His wife told him that she could not keep watching him suffer, that he deserved to have his life back. He agreed to come to therapy, though he does not believe much can change. He is terrified that the memories will never stop feeling so real, and he is equally terrified that letting his guard down will invite another disaster. He hopes, quietly, that maybe he can learn to rest again. He does not know how.
